subtitle: Journal-club style ICU update: PICO, key results, appraisal, bedside impact, and medical English.

script.heading: Intro
sentences: Welcome to Critical Care Daily for November 27, 2026.
Today we will review 3 recent ICU-relevant publications.
The format is quick listen first, then PICO, key results, critical appraisal, bedside impact, and medical English notes.
Use this as a morning triage tool, then open the source link for full-text appraisal before changing practice.

script.heading: Story 1 - Resuscitation strategies incorporating peripheral perfusion ta
sentences: Story 1 is about Resuscitation strategies incorporating peripheral perfusion targets in septic shock: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials..
This is a systematic review / meta-analysis from Journal of critical care.

The clinical question is best framed as follows: in Critically ill or ICU-relevant patients described in the abstract; confirm eligibility criteria in the full text., how should we interpret uncertain. We aimed to evaluate whether these strategies reduce 28/30-day mortality and improve other clinical outcomes compared with usual care. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) using a random-effects model wa?
Five RCTs involving 2180 patients with septic shock were included.

Compared with conventional strategies, RSIPPT were not associated with significant differences in 28/30-day mortality (four RCTs; RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.78-1.09; I2 = 10%; moderate CoE) or 90-day mortality (three RCTs; RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.83-1.05; I2 = 0%; low CoE).
However, RSIPPT were associated with fluid reduction during the first 6-8 h of resuscitation (three RCTs; MD -264.53 mL, 95% CI -425.28 to -103.77; I2 = 1%; low CoE).
For critical appraisal, focus on whether the design supports a causal conclusion and whether the patients resemble your ICU population.

The bedside implication is this: Potentially practice-relevant because a patient-centered outcome is reported; check absolute risk difference, adverse events, and whether your ICU population matches the study.
Useful English phrase: these findings should be interpreted cautiously because the details of design and applicability matter.

sentences: Story 2 is about Remimazolam versus propofol for sedation in mechanically ventilated ICU patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials..
This is a systematic review / meta-analysis from Journal of critical care.

The clinical question is best framed as follows: in ICU patients, how should we interpret Remimazolam compared with propofol for sedation in mechanically ventilated ICU patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials?
Six RCTs including 705 patients were analyzed.
No statistically significant difference was detected in the percentage of time within the target sedation range (MD, -0.45%; 95% CI, -2.46 to 1.55; p = 0.56; I2 = 0%).

No significant differences were detected in sedation success rate, 28-day mortality, ICU mortality, ICU length of stay, and duration of mechanical ventilation, or safety outcomes, although several estimates were imprecise.

articles.summary: Five RCTs involving 2180 patients with septic shock were included. However, RSIPPT were associated with fluid reduction during the first 6-8 h of resuscitation (three RCTs; MD -264.53 mL, 95% CI -425.28 to -103.77; I2 = 1%; low CoE). articles.title: Remimazolam versus propofol for sedation in mechanically ventilated ICU patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.summary: Continuous endpoints were reported using mean differences (MDs), and dichotomous outcomes were analyzed using risk ratios (RRs), with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Six RCTs including 705 patients were analyzed. No statistically significant difference was detected in the percentage of time within the target sedation range (MD, -0.45%; 95% CI, -2.46 to 1.55; p = 0.56; I2 = 0%). No significant differences were detected in sedation success rate, 28-day mortality, ICU mortality, ICU length of stay, and duration of mechanical ventilation, or safety outcomes, although several estimates were imprecise. Propofol is widely used for sedation in the intensive care unit (ICU), but its use may be limited by cardiovascular depression, hypertriglyceridemia, and propofol infusion syndrome.

articles.title: The association between normal capillary refill time and 28-day mortality in septic shock patients subjected to early hemodynamic resuscitation.
articles.summary: This post-hoc analysis included all randomized patients from the ANDROMEDA-SHOCK 1 and 2 trials. CRT was classified as normal (≤3 s) or abnormal (>3 s). The primary outcome was 28-day mortality, analyzed using Cox proportional hazards regression and reported as hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Among 1885 patients, 691 (36.7%) had normal baseline CRT. Despite normal CRT, many had abnormal hemodynamic features: 335 (48.5%) had heart rate > 100/min, 258 (37.3%) systolic arterial pressure < 100 mmHg, 152 (22.0%) mean arterial pressure < 65 mmHg, 157 (22.7%) diastolic arterial pressure < 50 mmHg, and 683 (98.8%) lactate >2 mmol/L.
